parts.text:
As for catching mice you lack merit, but I never complain,

A ladle of fish and rice will come at the

time.

Throughout the day I see you sleeping peacefully,

So why am I always coming and going?

Lu sees himself through the bemused eyes of the cat, who’s perhaps wondering why this foolish old man is rushing to and fro, fulfilling goals and seeking

, when he might just be satisfied with what he already has.

And despite his cat’s indolence, Lu continues to cherish his feline, making sure to regularly serve its dinner. This is significant, given that other premodern Chinese writers viewed cats

as vermin-catchers that should be replaced once they outlive their usefulness.

Personhood and care

Imagining oneself as a pampered cat will be familiar to those of us who live with cats – a thought-experiment that is

with more than a little envy for the capacity to live in the moment, without anxiety over the future.

Lu’s care for his cat affords him the possibility of imagining a nonhuman animal mind. The

learns something from his cat in the end, as he imagines the world through the cat’s eyes and, in doing so, perhaps finds a measure of solace.

Lu does not speak in the language of what philosophers call moral personhood. He is not reflecting on the broader

question of which creatures deserve to be treated with care and respect.

But I argue that his actions nonetheless demonstrate how he treats his cat as somewhat of an

. This can be seen, not least of all, by how he addresses poems to his cat, an act of social exchange that was heretofore reserved for literary interactions with other human beings.

Personhood – the recognition of an individual as deserving of dignity – is often assumed the sole

of human beings. But philosopher María Puig de la Bellacasa has promoted a worldview that she calls “more than human thinking,” which urges people to broaden their scope of moral concern, and in this way,

human capacities for care and love. The philosopher Lori Gruen similarly conceives of an “entangled empathy,” calling attention to the complex relational intimacies that bind human and nonhuman animals together. They insist that human
are better when the sphere of care and concern is extended to those creatures with whom human lives are entangled.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: The discovery of a Roman fort revives interest in an emperor's place in Welsh tradition.
Objects found at a medieval Irish fort reveal details of daily life and material culture.
Ancient disputes over mapmaking illuminate debates about how the world is represented.
A Chinese poet's writing about cats offers an early exploration of their imagined inner lives.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: Meanwhile, premodern poets, writers and artists were among the first to wonder about the inner lives of cats – and to explore how caring for them might expand our capacity for empathy.

questions.prompt: What evidence is given of ancient Egyptian affection for cats?
options: A complete absence of artistic representations
Sculptures, paintings and mummified remains
Satellite images of modern animal shelters
Only twentieth-century cinema advertisements
questions.explanation: 第 4 段提供了作答依据。正确选项用不同说法表达了文中的信息；请比较范围、数量、因果关系与限定词。
questions.evidence: Of course, the ancient Egyptians loved cats – this can be seen in sculptures, paintings and even mummified cat remains.
